Yes — and it's stronger than a single page. On the evidence it's a **layer**, not a node in a corner.

## It fails all eight existing types

Running your own CONVENTIONS §0 test on Tessl: it ships no methodology (not `framework`), it isn't an agent loop (not `harness`), it doesn't spawn loops (not `runtime`). The near-miss is `store`, and the way it misses is the useful part: a store holds state about **work the agent did** and is read *back* after a run; a registry holds **capabilities** and provisions the agent *before* one. Opposite direction, different content. So it's genuinely a ninth type.

## It's populated, which is the decisive bit

Not just Tessl: [JFrog](https://jfrog.com/ai-catalog/skills-registry/) ships a private signed-and-scanned skills registry (the canonical package-registry incumbent entering the space, with NVIDIA), [Google Cloud](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/build/skill-registry) ships a Skill Registry in Gemini Enterprise, plus ClawHub, [Agensi](https://www.agensi.io/learn/ai-agent-marketplace-landscape-2026), and Smithery on the MCP side. There's an emerging open format (AgentSkills, ~40 products on agentskills.io) and an OpenClaw registry protocol. An incumbent plus a hyperscaler plus a standard is the signature of a category. You minted `store` on two instances; this clears that bar comfortably.

[Tessl](https://tessl.io/) itself is the best anchor: $125M, Guy Podjarny (Snyk), 3,000+ skills — and it **paused its Framework product to become a registry**, which is a wiki-grade finding on its own.

## The real argument: it answers three things the wiki has already left open

1. **`bm-skills` is currently miscategorized.** It's paged as a `framework` and its own page says it *isn't* one — it's a plugin marketplace. This layer gives it a correct home.
2. **`topic-ai-native-sdlc.md:60` claims continuous evals of the agent's configuration are an instrument "no community framework in the wiki ships."** Tessl's Task Evals ships exactly that commercially. Not a falsification — a sharpening. The instrument exists; it just doesn't live in a *framework*, it lives in a layer you haven't paged yet.
3. **It's evidence the framework is unbundling into its capabilities.** Your whole ontology says a framework is a bundle of `capability` pages. A registry makes the capability the independently versioned, installable unit. pstack ships inside Cursor's marketplace, Superpowers has its own — the bundle is becoming a distribution convenience. That's a synthesis finding the wiki exists to surface.

A weaker fourth: registries enforce mechanically-gated policy, which bears on the parked `stage-govern` candidate — but it doesn't clear that trigger (the trigger asks for a *framework* gating *project principles*; this is a platform gating a *skill corpus*). It suggests govern may be substrate rather than stage. Worth noting, not claiming.

## The boundary you'd have to decide

The hard case is harness-vendor marketplaces — Anthropic's, `cursor/plugins`, opencode's registry. My proposed rule, mirroring your existing harness/runtime test: **an independent, cross-harness product is a `registry`; a marketplace shipped by a harness vendor stays a harness feature and a matrix row.** Otherwise you double-count and the layer sprawls into MCP registries and general agent marketplaces.

On naming, `registry` fits the house style, and your "A note on the word" precedent for `runtime` handles the fact that the products have outgrown the term — Tessl is registry *plus* governance, evals, observability, inventory. The layer would be "the supply layer," the node `registry`, with `subtype: public | private` and edges roughly `distributes:` → capability/framework and `integrates_with:` → harness.

## Cost, and a cheaper option

This is a ninth namespace: CONVENTIONS surgery, new edges, catalogue and index restructure, plus the `bm-skills` re-filing. Bigger than the pstack ingest.

The cheaper move is to write `topic-skill-supply-chain` first — a curated overlay costs you nothing structurally, spans ≥3 namespaces so it passes the topic gate, and lets you see the layer assembled before committing the schema. That's the "park it until the evidence demands it" discipline you've applied twice already.

My honest read: the evidence already demands the node, and the topic would be a detour. But it's your schema, and the boundary rule above is the call I'd want you to make rather than me.

**The main decision: the Factory is filed as a framework, not a runtime.** It calls itself a software factory, but it ships only instructions. The scheduler, connectors, worktrees and credentials all come from the agent host, so it never launches agents itself. By this wiki's rule that means it isn't a runtime. **What the Factory adds to the wiki:**
- **It fills an empty cell in the software-factory topic.** The design grid there had no example of a factory whose control plane lives in the prompt (the direct opposite of `sssf`). The topic page now has a new section and a 🧩 marker for this case.
- **A new pattern, `pattern-action-gating`.** The Factory splits authority into ten separate permissions: fix, reply, close, review, approve, publish, merge, deploy, recover and notify. One never implies another. Evidence is tied to the exact PR head and expires after a required waiting period ("soak") if anything changes. gh-aw enforces the same split through its CI job structure, and the two are cross-linked as opposite ends of one approach.
- **A new artifact, `artifact-autonomy-policy`.** This is the `.agent-factory/config.yaml` file. It sets what the agent may *do*, where the existing constitution and standards pages cover design and conventions.
